title: Plus factors: combining your background into one offer
audience: Teachers, trainers and owners of any service business who want an offer that draws on more than one part of their background.
learningOutcomes: List plus factors across five areas of work, study, interests, life experience and community ties, and mark the evidence for each
Combine two or three plus factors into one offer statement that names a client group and a result
Test each combination for a named buyer and for the business's ability to deliver it

instruction.heading: Distinct offers often combine several things
instruction.body: Most people can name one skill. A stronger offer often combines several things at once: work from an earlier career, a training path, an interest that shows up in the service, a language, or a local connection. When two or three of these meet in one service, the result is harder to copy, because nobody else has the same mix. The aim is a combination that a particular group of clients would recognise as useful. A list of achievements is not the aim.

instruction.heading: Build an honest inventory
instruction.body: Write down your plus factors across five areas: work history, study and training, interests and hobbies, life experience, and community or language ties. For each item, note the evidence you hold: a certificate, a client reference, a portfolio, dated work records or a clear personal account. An item with no evidence can still be part of your story, but it must not be presented as a credential or a result.

instruction.heading: Combine two or three factors into one offer
instruction.body: Pick the combinations that point at a client group and a result. For example, a former teacher who also does handyman work could offer after-hours repairs to families with young children, with a short walk-through of the home beforehand. Test each combination with two questions. Would a specific group pay for it? Can you deliver it well? A bundle that nobody would buy is a hobby, however interesting it is.

instruction.heading: Keep each combination inside what you are qualified to do
instruction.body: Combining factors can make an offer sound more expert than it is. Describe only the training and experience you hold, and do not let a plus factor imply a trade qualification, licence or clinical role you do not have. Where a combined service involves licensed work, the licence rules have not yet been confirmed in this lesson and must be checked with the relevant state or territory authority before you advertise the service.

procedure: Write plus factors across the five areas: work, study, interests, life experience, and community or language ties
Attach one piece of evidence to each factor you intend to use publicly, and mark any factor without evidence as personal story only
Write three to five combinations of two or three factors
Test each combination against a named client group and your ability to deliver it
Choose one combination, write its sentence, and check that every claim matches your evidence and your licence position

workedExamples.situation: Nadia, a former bookkeeper who now teaches a community yoga class, asks whether her two backgrounds can form one offer for small cafes and shopfronts.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the combination an offer, and what should she check first?
workedExamples.reasoning: The combination could suit business owners who want a calm reset away from the numbers. She should evidence her bookkeeping experience with dated work and client references, and describe the class as her own practice and teaching, not as a clinical service. She should test the offer with three business owners before she prints anything.

workedExamples.situation: Dimitri is a painter who trained as a joiner. He wants to offer repainting of heritage timber trim for owners of older homes.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which claim can he make about his joinery training, and what licence question remains?
workedExamples.reasoning: He can describe joinery training only with the certificate or course record in hand. He should say he repaints timber trim, not that he restores heritage structures, unless he holds evidence for that work.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is needed for this lesson
Certificates, course records, work references and a portfolio folder
A notebook for the plus factor inventory

commonErrors.error: Listing every achievement, so the offer has no focus
commonErrors.prevention: Keep only the factors that point at one client group and one result.

commonErrors.error: Letting an old job title stand in for evidence
commonErrors.prevention: Check each title against a dated record or reference before it appears in advertising.

commonErrors.error: Using a combination that implies a licence or clinical role
commonErrors.prevention: State only what you hold, and check licence status before advertising licensed work.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Describing a qualification, licence or experience you do not hold may mislead clients, and misleading claims are regulated under the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC's general guidance on false or misleading claims applies here; it does not address combined offers specifically.

Licence notice: this lesson does not grant, confirm or replace any licence or trade qualification. Where a combined offer includes licensed work, the licence requirement has not yet been confirmed and must be checked with the relevant state or territory authority.

qualityStandard: Each plus factor used publicly has a named evidence item
Each combined offer names one client group, one result and one delivery method
No credential, licence or clinical role is implied that the business does not hold
documentationEvidence: Plus factor inventory with an evidence reference for each factor used
Chosen combination sentence and the date it was tested
Licence check record, or a note that the check is still pending
summary: A distinctive offer often combines two or three factors from work, study, life and community
Keep an evidence reference for every factor you use in public
Test each combination for a named buyer and for your ability to deliver it
A combination must not imply a credential or licence the business does not hold

knowledgeChecks.question: Which description of a plus factor is the most accurate?
options: An experience that can set an offer apart when it is combined with others
Any certificate you hold, whether or not you use it, and anything you have studied
A discount you offer to first-time clients and the free parking you offer

knowledgeChecks.question: Which is the safest way to use a past experience on a website?
options: Describe it as a qualification even though you did not complete the course
Describe only what you can show, such as dates, work done or a training record
Describe any experience the client may find impressive

knowledgeChecks.question: A combined offer has been chosen. What is the next check?
options: Print the bundle on business cards and hand them out at the gym today
Charge a premium before any client has tried it and put it in a bigger font on the sign
Confirm that a named group would want the combination, and that you can deliver it
